title: Moses Mendelssohn
hook: a Berlin philosopher who translated the Torah into German

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mussar begins: a shoemaker's candle, and Salanter's idea that there's still time to mend. Your line was work on yourself. Did you catch your one trait? Today we leave Eastern Europe for Berlin, and a new part of the story. Day nine hundred seventy-one.

The challenge is printed on the first pages of a book, where anyone can read it. A Swiss pastor named Johann Caspar Lavater has dedicated the book to a Jewish philosopher in Berlin, and in the dedication he challenges him in public: either show what is wrong with Christianity, or do what reason demands and be baptized. Readers are watching. The philosopher is admired in the salons, praised by Christian friends, read in German. And now he has been handed a choice between attacking his neighbors' faith and leaving his own. His name is Moses Mendelssohn, and his answer is today's story.
screen: `A PUBLIC CHALLENGE.` → `REFUTE IT, OR BE BAPTIZED.` → `READERS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Mendelssohn took a third way. He wrote back, publicly, that he remained firm in his own faith, and that he had no wish to go to war against anyone else's. Judaism, he explained, does not go out looking for converts, and he did not want to spend his life in religious dispute. He would keep his faith and keep his friends. That answer is Mendelssohn in miniature: a man living in two worlds and refusing to give either one up. He was an observant Jew who kept the commandments, and a German philosopher who wrote in elegant German about God, the soul and beauty. Then he did something to bring those two worlds into one room. He translated the Torah into German, and had it printed in Hebrew letters, alongside the Hebrew text and a Hebrew commentary. A young Jew who read Hebrew could open the Torah and, line by line, learn a careful German too. There is an old rabbinic way of thinking about that kind of bridge. In Genesis, Noah blesses Shem and Japheth, saying: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem." The Talmud, in tractate Megillah, reads that verse as permission to write the Torah in Greek, letting the beauty of Japheth live inside the tents of Shem. Mendelssohn's translation was a similar wager: that the beauty of a new language could live inside the Torah's tent without knocking it down. Not everyone agreed. Some rabbis worried his translation would lead young people toward German and away from Torah. Others welcomed it. Both reactions are part of his story.
screen: `A THIRD WAY: FIRM, AND AT PEACE.` · `AN OBSERVANT JEW, A GERMAN PHILOSOPHER.` · `THE TORAH IN GERMAN, IN HEBREW LETTERS.` · then, large: `JAPHETH IN THE TENTS OF SHEM.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: bridge two worlds you live in. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Name two worlds you move between. Work and home. The language of your parents and the language of your friends. A faith community and a secular office. Two countries. Picture each one as a room. Notice what you usually leave at the door when you go from one to the other. Then ask: is there one small thing from the first room that could come into the second, without breaking either? Just find it. The bell holds the time.
Moses Mendelssohn. A Berlin philosopher and observant Jew who translated the Torah into German, in Hebrew letters, and answered a public challenge by staying firm in his own faith. Today's word.
Your line: two worlds. Today, carry one thing from one of your worlds into the other: a word, a habit, a kindness. Day nine hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Mendelssohn's German translation of the Torah, with its Hebrew commentary known as the Biur, is studied by historians as a turning point, and his life is often discussed in Jewish schools as a model and a question about living in two cultures.
